newsitem.title: BELGIUM: German unification costs raise possible EMU fudge.
newsitem.headline: German unification costs raise possible EMU fudge.

text.p: Germany, plagued by heavy debt related to unification, might be able to turn the cost to its advantage, using it as a way to squeeze in to the single European currency, EU officials and analysts said on Monday.
The first hint of such a strategy came at a meeting of European Union finance ministers which gave Germany high marks on its economic convergence programme for the single currency, expected in 1999.

German officials, led by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, argued that their debt level, which has been rising steadily in recent years as a percentage of GDP, had been heavily influenced by the massive costs associated with German unification in 1990.
Countries wishing to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) must demonstrate that their debt ratios are declining and approaching 60 percent of GDP at a satisfactory pace.
The problem for Germany is that its ratio has been rising and is projected at 61.5 percent in 1997.
Bonn's argument, accepted by all members in the 15-nation bloc, is that unification represented an extraordinary event that saddled it with costs of a one-time nature.

What some EU officials speculated about on Monday is the possibility that Germany could also argue that the interest costs associated with the unification debt should also be taken into account when calculating its budget deficits.
"If they accept exceptional circumstances on debt you would have to accept exceptional circumstances which allows for interest outlays," said one EU monetary official.
Under such a scenario, the potential savings could be enormous.

A rough calculation, using 400 billion marks ($235.9 billion) in unificiation-related debt and a five percent interest rate, would put the budgetary savings at 20 billion, easily allowing Bonn to meet Maastricht's three percent to GDP ratio.
Is such a strategy possible?

Officials said under Article 104C, which includes a clause specifying that "all other relevant factors" must be taken into account when assessing whether a country has meet the criteria, Germany might claim an exceptional circumstance.
The idea is controversial at the least and could fling the door open to many so-called exceptional events, analysts said.
"Germany could credibly claim that its fiscal malaise was due to a one-off event," said Holger Schmeiding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
"The big problem is that this is a fudge and if Germany has to ask for one then it is in no position to disallow it for others."
The ultimate nightmare scenario for Germany under such a plan is a monetary union with many members, an outcome that would likely weaken the credibility of the new currency at the start in 1999.

Other analysts said the the deficit criteria has taken on such great importance for Bonn that to manipulate it in such a way would undermine its credibility and ability to sell the merits of EMU within Germany.
"The fact is that the German government has raised the level of the deficit criteria well beyond the importance the treaty gives it," said Bruce Kasman, economist at J.P. Morgan in London.

"If you start fudging the deficit numbers for a country like Germany, then you have a much harder time at the end of the day to say to a country like Italy that you are going to have to wait," he added.
($ = 1.695 German Marks)
